items.followUp: What is a compound? Explain how it differs from an element.

rubric.why: An element consists of one kind of atom and cannot be decomposed into simpler substances by chemical means.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for a complete definition. Award 1 mark for identifying it as a pure substance made of one kind of atom or stating that it cannot be decomposed chemically.

rubric.why: Metals are a kind of element and are generally good conductors of heat and electricity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming metals and giving a suitable characteristic or example.

rubric.why: Non-metals are a kind of element and are generally poor conductors of heat and electricity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming non-metals and giving a suitable characteristic or example.

rubric.why: Metalloids have properties intermediate between those of metals and non-metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming metalloids and stating that their properties are intermediate, or giving a suitable example.

modelAnswer: An element is a pure substance made up of only one kind of atom and cannot be decomposed into simpler substances by chemical means.
Elements are classified into three kinds:
Metals are generally lustrous and good conductors of heat and electricity; examples are iron and copper.
Non-metals are generally poor conductors of heat and electricity; examples are oxygen and sulphur.
Metalloids have properties intermediate between metals and non-metals; silicon is an example.

items.followUp: What is a covalent bond? Give an example of each of its three types.

rubric.why: A covalent bond forms when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a covalent bond is formed by sharing one or more pairs of electrons between atoms.

rubric.why: A single covalent bond consists of one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that one pair of electrons is shared or giving a correct example such as H₂.

rubric.why: A double covalent bond consists of two shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that two pairs of electrons are shared or giving a correct example such as O₂.

rubric.why: A triple covalent bond consists of three shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that three pairs of electrons are shared or giving a correct example such as N₂.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
A single covalent bond is formed by sharing one pair of electrons, for example, H₂.
A double covalent bond is formed by sharing two pairs of electrons, for example, O₂.
A triple covalent bond is formed by sharing three pairs of electrons, for example, N₂.

items.followUp: State the main conclusions drawn from Rutherford’s gold foil experiment.

rubric.why: The experiment directed a beam of alpha particles from a source at a thin sheet of gold.
rubric.description: Identifies the particles and gold foil used.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing alpha particles directed at a thin gold foil.

rubric.why: The radioactive source and shielding or collimation provided a narrow beam of alpha particles.
rubric.description: Describes production of the alpha-particle beam.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the source and a narrow beam, or explaining how it was produced.

rubric.why: A fluorescent screen detected the alpha particles by producing flashes where they struck.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a fluorescent screen, such as a zinc sulphide screen, as the detector.

rubric.why: Most alpha particles passed through the foil without deflection.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that most alpha particles passed straight through without deflection.

rubric.why: Some alpha particles were deflected, while a very small number bounced back.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a few particles were deflected or that very few bounced back.

modelAnswer: A narrow beam of alpha particles from a radioactive source was directed at a very thin gold foil.
A fluorescent zinc sulphide screen around the foil detected the alpha particles by producing flashes where they struck.
Observations:
Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without any deflection.
A few alpha particles were deflected, while a very few bounced back.

items.followUp: Explain how temperature and humidity affect the rate of evaporation.

rubric.why: Evaporation is a surface change from liquid to vapour that occurs below the boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining evaporation as a change from liquid to vapour at the surface below the boiling point.

rubric.why: Higher temperature gives particles more energy to escape from the liquid surface, increasing the rate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing temperature increases the rate of evaporation, preferably with a reason.

rubric.why: A larger exposed surface allows more particles to escape at the same time.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of surface area.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing the exposed surface area increases the rate of evaporation.

rubric.why: Moving air removes vapour from above the liquid, and low humidity allows more vapour to enter the air.
rubric.description: Explains the effects of wind and humidity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly explaining the effect of wind or humidity; the full answer should mention both.

modelAnswer: Evaporation is the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface at a temperature below its boiling point.
Higher temperature increases the rate of evaporation because more particles have enough energy to escape.
A larger surface area increases the rate because more particles are exposed at the surface.
Higher wind speed increases evaporation by carrying vapour away; low humidity also increases evaporation because the air can take up more vapour.

items.followUp: Distinguish between a saturated solution and an unsaturated solution at a given temperature.

rubric.why: An unsaturated solution contains less than the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at that temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at the stated temperature.

rubric.why: The example applies the definition to a sodium thiosulphate solution that can still dissolve more solute.
rubric.description: Gives the sodium thiosulphate example for an unsaturated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a sodium thiosulphate solution to which more solute can still be added and dissolved at that temperature.

rubric.why: A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution normally holds at the same temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it contains more dissolved sodium thiosulphate than a saturated solution can normally hold at that temperature.

rubric.why: Careful cooling of a hot saturated sodium thiosulphate solution can produce a supersaturated solution, which may crystallise if disturbed or seeded.
rubric.description: Gives the sodium thiosulphate example for a supersaturated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a hot saturated sodium thiosulphate solution cooled carefully; noting that it may crystallise on disturbance or seeding is also acceptable.

modelAnswer: An unsaturated solution contains less solute than the maximum amount that can dissolve at a given temperature, so it can dissolve more sodium thiosulphate at that temperature.
A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution normally holds at the same temperature.
For example, an unsaturated sodium thiosulphate solution can dissolve more solute.
A hot saturated sodium thiosulphate solution, cooled carefully without crystallisation, becomes supersaturated; it may crystallise if disturbed or seeded.

items.followUp: Write the chemical formulae of carbon dioxide and calcium chloride.

rubric.why: The chemical formula of water is H₂O.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for H₂O.

rubric.why: The chemical formula of sodium hydroxide, or caustic soda, is NaOH.
rubric.description: Writes the formula of sodium hydroxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for NaOH.

modelAnswer: (a) Water: H₂O
(b) Sodium hydroxide (caustic soda): NaOH
